title: India warns AI-powered hackers targeting crypto exchanges at ‘machine speed’
summary: India’s cybersecurity agency says a threat actor is escalating an AI-assisted hacking campaign targeting crypto exchanges and other financial firms.
content: India's cybersecurity agency has issued a warning regarding an escalating threat campaign. Officials state that AI-powered hackers are targeting cryptocurrency exchanges and other financial institutions at unprecedented speeds. This sophisticated, machine-speed cyber activity poses a significant risk to the security of digital asset platforms and requires heightened vigilance from organizations across the financial sector.

title: Finalytics.ai Launches a Personalized Digital Experience for Travis Credit Union
summary:
Finalytics.ai, the behavioral intelligence and personalization platform for community banks and credit unions, today announced the launch of a personalized digital experience for Travis Credit Union, built around what each member is trying to accomplish. Whether someone is opening their first account, shopping for an auto loan or exploring ways to save, the credit union’s website now recognizes that need and responds to it, instead of showing every person the same page.
The change reflects a simple idea at the center of how Travis serves its 280,000 members: no two members are in the same place, and the credit union should meet each of them where they are. In a branch, a Travis team member listens first and then helps. The personalized experience brings that same approach online.
For members, the difference shows up in small, practical ways. A young adult researching their first credit card sees plain-language guidance on building credit rather than a wall of products. A family comparing auto loans sees the rate, the monthly payment and a clear path to pre-approval. Each person spends less time hunting and more time getting the thing done that brought them there.
“Our members know what it feels like to walk into a Travis branch and be recognized. We wanted the same thing online. Every member should feel that the experience was built for them, because it was. This is about listening to what each person needs and making it easier for them to reach their goals,” said Grant Karsas, Vice President, Digital Experience at Travis Credit Union.
Finalytics delivered the experience with its platform, which recognizes what a person is looking for from how they move through the credit union’s website, and adjusts the content, offers and next steps accordingly. Finalytics also supports the Travis team with the copy, offers and reporting behind the experience, and measures success in the outcomes that matter to members and the credit union: accounts opened and loans funded.
“Travis started from the member’s point of view and worked backward. The question was never what the technology could do, it was what a member standing in front of us would need, and how the website could answer that first. That is the right way to think about personalization, and the Travis team held us to it,” said Craig McLaughlin, Founder and CEO of Finalytics.ai.
The personalized experience is live now across Travis’s website, and the credit union will continue to refine it based on how members use it.

title: 58% of UK Adults Not Ready to Let AI Manage Their Money, Despite Widespread Use, FIS Research Finds
summary:
UK consumers are already using artificial intelligence (AI) for help with their money, but most are not ready to let it take control. They want firm spending limits, a guaranteed refund and a person who can step in before they will trust AI to act on their behalf. This is according to new research from global financial technology leader FIS®.
The 2026 FIS Consumer Pulse Survey of 2,000 UK adults found that 58% are not ready to hand their day-to-day money management to an AI assistant. Only 22% say they are ready, compared with 37% in the US. Despite this, many consumers are happy to use AI as a helper. More than half (58%) have turned to GenAI tools such as ChatGPT or Claude in the past 12 months for tasks like budgeting, answering a question about their account or choosing a financial product, and 64% expect to in the next 12 months.
Adoption is real, but letting go is not
UK consumers are already bringing AI into their financial lives. As well as general GenAI tools, 56% have used an AI assistant within their banking app for something to do with their money in the past year. But using AI to answer a question or plan a budget is different from letting it act. Half (51%) of UK adults have never heard of agentic banking, in which AI carries out banking tasks on a customer’s behalf.
Readiness to hand over day-to-day money management is low across every generation. Millennials (33%) are the most ready, followed by Gen Z (27%), Gen X (15%), adults aged 62 to 69 (8%) and those aged 70 and older (3%). Young UK adults are significantly less likely to indicate readiness to as their US counterparts, where 61% of Millennials and 58% of Gen Z say they are ready.
The findings come as UK banks and regulators begin testing AI that acts for customers. The Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) AI Live Testing service, whose second cohort began testing in April 2026, includes firms trialing agentic payments, and on 19 October 2026 the FCA published examples of good and poor practice for AI in financial services. As AI moves from pilot to product, consumers will help set the pace.
Kanv Pandit, Head of International Markets – Banking and Payments, at FIS said: “UK consumers aren’t rejecting AI, and most are already using it to help with their finances, but they aren’t ready to give up control. The message for banks is clear: start with the tasks people already welcome, like stopping a suspicious charge, let customers set the limits and be clear about who is accountable when something goes wrong. Banks that get this right will earn consumers’ trust to let AI do more on their behalf.”
Drawing the line on what AI can do
Comfort with AI depends on the task. UK adults are most comfortable with an AI assistant flagging or freezing a suspicious charge (56%), paying a recurring bill they have approved before (52%) and rounding up purchases into savings (51%). Comfort falls for sending money to another person or business (38%), opening a new savings or deposit account (35%) and applying for a loan or credit card (30%).
UK adults also want tight limits on spending. More than half (56%) would not let an AI assistant in their banking app spend or move any money without approving the transaction. Among those who would, 35% would cap it at £250 or less, and just 5% of all UK adults would allow more than £500 or set no limit.
Consumers are writing the terms for AI
UK consumers are clear about what it would take to trust AI with their money. 62% rank a guaranteed refund for any mistake among their top three conditions, higher than in the US (58%) and Singapore (57%), followed by a person who can review or override decisions (51%), and a strong security and fraud-protection track record (47%).
Among those not ready to hand over day-to-day money management, 64% say they want to stay in control of their own money, 50% don’t trust AI to get it right and 48% worry it could make costly mistakes.
Pandit added: “The UK is telling banks exactly what trustworthy AI looks like. Consumers want a refund if something goes wrong, a person who can step in and the freedom to set their own limits. Trust is the deciding factor for whether consumers let AI act on their behalf, and it has to be earned before AI acts, not repaired afterwards. That means building safeguards in from the start. FIS Orchestrated Intelligence is designed to do exactly that. It works within the limits customers set, explains its decisions and keeps a person in the loop so trust is assured before AI acts on anyone’s behalf. Banks that put trust first will be the ones consumers allow to do more.”

title: Half of UK Consumers Willing to Switch to Islamic Finance
summary:
Half of UK consumers (50%) have shared that they would be willing to switch from conventional banking to Islamic finance if it offered comparable services, according to new research published by Gatehouse Bank.
The Islamic finance industry is one of the fastest growing areas of financial services globally, predicted to grow to over US$4 trillion in assets by 2030, from a market of US$200 billion in 2003. This global growth opportunity is complemented by strong consumer demand in the UK, with Shariah-compliant products and services proving popular among consumers of all religions or of no religion.
The Bank’s new research follows two years after the publication of its Islamic and Ethical Finance Consumer Report, which examined perceptions, awareness and understanding of Islamic, ethical and green finance in the UK. Not only does the latest research show a continued willingness to switch but awareness of Islamic finance remains strong, with over two fifths (41%) of respondents stating that they have at least some knowledge of the industry.
The UK’s Islamic finance industry has been growing over recent years and is now home to approximately 20 institutions providing Islamic finance products, including five fully Shariah-compliant banks.
Motivating factors
When asked what would motivate them to choose Islamic finance, respondents cited alignment with their value system and beliefs (19%) and that providers are trustworthy and transparent (18%) as the most important factors. This rises considerably among Muslim consumers, with over a third (34%) choosing Islamic finance due to its alignment with their value system and beliefs, followed by a similar number of people (30%) who said that providers are trustworthy and transparent.
Interestingly, the research found that consumers who are willing to make the switch to an Islamic finance provider were motivated by similar factors, regardless of their age group.
Knowledge of Islamic finance among UK consumers matches that of ethical and green finance
There remains a strong appetite for Islamic, ethical and green finance among UK consumers, as 41% of respondents had at least some awareness of Islamic finance. This closely correlates with ethical finance (38%) and green finance (37%), highlighting the strong alignment between the Shariah principles and sustainable and ethical practices.
Unsurprisingly, Muslim consumers were more likely to have at least some awareness of Islamic finance, with over three fifths (63%) stating this. However, Muslim consumers were also much more likely to be knowledgeable about green finance (51%) and ethical finance (55%) too, further highlighting the interconnectedness between these types of alternative finance products.
Knowledge gap among older generations
A finding consistent with Gatehouse Bank’s 2024 report is that those aged 45+ were much less likely to have knowledge of Islamic, ethical or green finance and the least likely to be open to switching to an Islamic finance provider. This is particularly prevalent for those aged 55+, with only just over 1 in 10 (11%) willing to make the switch. In comparison, over 6 in 10 (65%) of those aged 25-44 would be open to switching, followed closely by over 5 in 10 (55%) of those aged 18-24.
This highlights an opportunity for alternative finance providers to provide better education and provisions for older generations to ensure they are not missing out on what alternative finance providers have to offer.
Andy Homer, Chief Customer Officer at Gatehouse Bank, commented: “It is encouraging to see that UK consumers are increasingly willing to consider alternatives to conventional banking and are placing greater importance on choosing financial providers that align with their personal values.
“As the Islamic finance sector continues to grow, both in the UK and around the world, consumers are benefiting from greater choice and accessibility. At Gatehouse Bank, we welcome this and are proud to play our part by offering transparent, ethical products that are open to everyone, regardless of their religious background.”
*Research was commissioned by Gatehouse Bank and carried out by Censuswide. The survey anonymously surveyed 2,001 UK respondents, aged 18+ living in the UK between 28 September – 2 October 2026. Comparable services were defined as the selection of products, online services, customer support, pricing and ease of access.

title: Zilch Reports $300M Annual Run Rate Off the Back of Strong FY26 Results
summary:
Zilch, the consumer payments app, has reached a $300m annual run rate and delivered two consecutive quarters of adjusted profit before tax in FY27 building on strong FY26 results announced today.
The results illustrate a year of strategic investments into the business with Zilch growing revenue 36% to £147.5m and GMV 28% to £2.4bn, while strengthening its products, technology, regulatory capabilities and brand. These investments laid the foundations for the acceleration now being seen in FY27, as the business delivers stronger revenue growth and improving underlying profitability.
Strong financial performance and growing customer engagement
Zilch delivered another year of strong financial performance in FY26, with gross profit increasing 24% to £65.6m and its revenue take rate rising from 5.98% to 6.34%, reflecting improved monetisation across the platform. Credit revenue grew 47% to £108.4m, while feature and advertising revenue increased 120% and 12% respectively, highlighting the growing contribution of additional revenue streams.
This performance was supported by continued growth in Zilch’s customer base and engagement. Yearly active users increased 21% to 970,000, while average annual spend per active customer rose 6% to £2,500. With customers making an average of 56 purchases a year, Zilch is becoming increasingly embedded in everyday spending, providing a strong foundation for continued growth.
A foundational year of strategic investment
Alongside its financial performance, FY26 was a year of deliberate investment as Zilch strengthened its products, technology and infrastructure to support its next phase of growth.
Zilch expanded its consumer proposition through new products and services, including physical cards, more flexible payment options and membership tiers, giving customers greater choice and flexibility. For merchants, the continued development of Intelligent Commerce, which uses data and AI to help brands reach customers and measure sales outcomes, further strengthened Zilch’s ambition to re-engineer the relationship between consumers and retailers.
The business also strengthened its financial and regulatory capabilities, increasing its securitisation facility to £200m, led by Deutsche Bank and supported by two of the world’s largest credit funds, providing capacity for approximately £4bn in annual GMV. Zilch ended FY26 with £106.5m in cash and secured its own FCA payments licence and Visa Principal Membership, strengthening its payments infrastructure and operational capabilities.
Together with its proposed acquisition of Fjord Bank, subject to regulatory approval, these developments have positioned Zilch to scale its operations, broaden its offering and pursue opportunities for international expansion.
Further investment to support the next phase of growth 
With the investments and strategic progress made during FY26 already translating into stronger financial performance in FY27, Zilch is continuing to invest in its UK presence and long-term growth. The company recently announced a £77m investment over ten years in a new London headquarters, which it will relocate to in 2027, providing additional capacity for its expanding workforce. Alongside its partnership with Arsenal Football Club, this reinforces Zilch’s commitment to the UK and its ambitions for the next phase of the business.

Philip Belamant, CEO and Co-Founder of Zilch, said:
“FY26 was a foundational year for Zilch. We delivered strong financial growth while making deliberate investments in our products, technology and infrastructure to strengthen the business and position ourselves for the next phase of expansion.
“We’re confident in the strength and profitability of our business model, and we’re now seeing the results of those investments. Reaching a $300m annual run rate and delivering two consecutive quarters of adjusted profit before tax demonstrates how the foundations we built during FY26 are translating into accelerated growth and stronger financial performance.
“Our ambition has always been to fundamentally change the relationship between consumers and brands, creating a more rewarding and transparent way for people to pay while delivering greater value for merchants. With a stronger platform, an expanding proposition and growing customer engagement, we’re already successfully building on this momentum.”

title: Amazon Seller Wallet GBP Launches, Giving Sellers in the UK Store More Control Over Their Money
summary:
Amazon today announced the launch of Amazon Seller Wallet GBP, giving eligible sellers a simpler way to manage proceeds earned through Amazon.co.uk.
Available directly within Seller Central, Seller Wallet GBP allows sellers based in the UK or overseas to hold funds in pounds sterling, pay UK suppliers directly and transfer money quickly to a UK bank account. GBP transfers to UK bank accounts are fast and free, giving sellers simpler access to funds for domestic business needs.
For sellers based outside of the UK, Seller Wallet GBP provides additional benefits when it comes to converting proceeds and managing their cashflow, enabling sellers to retain proceeds in GBP to pay UK suppliers or convert and send funds internationally in more than 20 currencies.
“Selling in the UK and internationally creates exciting growth opportunities, but it can also add complexity to everyday financial operations,” said Manasi Kudtarkar, General Manager of Amazon Seller Wallet. “With Seller Wallet GBP, we are giving sellers more choice and control over how they manage their UK proceeds, all from the same place they manage their business on Amazon.”
Key benefits for sellers:
Manage funds within Seller Central: Hold GBP proceeds earned through Amazon.co.uk, view balances, initiate transfers, and track the movement of funds alongside other business activities on Amazon.
Flexible transfer options: Make a one-time transfer or set up recurring schedules to send a fixed amount to your bank account weekly, every two weeks, or monthly.
See the full cost before transferring internationally: Review the exchange rate and total cost before confirming a transfer. A volume-based fee applies to international transfers and decreases as a seller's business with Amazon grows, with competitive exchange rates and no hidden markups or additional costs.
Simplify reporting and reconciliation: Access statements and transfer history within Seller Central to support cash-flow management, tax preparation, and account reconciliation.
The Seller Wallet experiences for GBP, EUR and USD are all separate and eligible sellers can enrol directly through Seller Central in a few clicks at no cost. Sellers operating in UK and EU stores can sign up for both GBP and EUR wallets at the same time using a streamlined process, while maintaining separate balances for each currency.
Seller Wallet first launched globally for the U.S. store in 2022, allowing sellers to manage and convert USD into more than 20 currencies in one place, before expanding in 2025 to seven European stores for global sellers to consolidate and manage EUR proceeds.

title: Yuno Chooses Ecommpay to Expand Payment Method Coverage Across Europe and Asia-Pacific

The partnership gives Yuno merchants a wider range of payment methods to improve checkout performance in key international markets, including local payment methods across selected European and Asia-Pacific markets.

The partnership focuses on enterprise merchants in retail and subscription, where fast time to market and broad local coverage matter most.
 
“Enterprise merchants shouldn’t have to choose between global reach and local performance,” said Mauricio Schwartzmann, Chief Financial Services Officer, Yuno. “With Ecommpay on Yuno, merchants can go live faster with the payment methods their customers expect across Europe and Asia-Pacific, backed by Ecommpay’s in-house fraud prevention. One integration, broader coverage and stronger performance in every target market.”
 
Roy Blokker, Head of Commercial at Ecommpay added: "Yuno and Ecommpay share a mission to help businesses navigate and thrive in a fast-changing e-commerce landscape. Together we have built a portfolio that gives Yuno merchants a greater range of payment methods, reducing drop-offs when customers don’t see a familiar way to pay at checkout.”
 
Yuno connects merchants to 1,000+ payment methods, providers and fraud tools in more than 190 countries and territories through one API (availability varies by market and provider). Because Yuno does not acquire, every routing decision is driven by transaction performance data alone.

title: The Payments Association Launches Payments Manifesto Setting Out UK Priorities to 2030
summary:
The Payments Association, a trade group representing the payments sector, has published The Payments Manifesto 2027, setting out a national strategy for trusted, competitive and innovative payments by 2030. The manifesto calls for payments to be recognised as critical national infrastructure, alongside sectors such as energy, telecommunications and transport.   
Aimed at government, regulators and industry leaders, the Manifesto draws on engagement with The Payments Association’s membership and has been reviewed by its Advisory Board. It builds on the Government’s National Payments Vision, setting out practical priorities to support progress towards 2030. 
The Payments Manifesto 2027: A national strategy for trusted, competitive and innovative payments by 2030 is structured around four interconnected national objectives.  
Growth, Competitiveness and Resilience focuses on modernising UK payments infrastructure through interoperability and resilience, while creating the conditions for payments businesses to grow and compete internationally.  
Trust, Security and Consumer Protection calls for earlier fraud prevention through intelligence sharing and accountability across the fraud chain, alongside improvements in financial inclusion, capability and meaningful payment choice.  
AI, Data and Digital Infrastructure seeks trusted rules for secure and accountable agentic payments, supported by internationally interoperable standards for agentic commerce.  
The future of Money and Payments calls for coherent, proportionate and internationally interoperable regulation for next-generation payments, including stablecoins and tokenised money.  
Nick Kerigan, Chair of The Payments Association’s Advisory Board and Managing Director, Head of Innovation at Swift, emphasised that payments are the invisible infrastructure of the UK economy. He highlighted that the Manifesto combines policy recommendations with The Payments Association’s commitment to convene expertise, build evidence and test proposals against real market experience. He also pointed to the Manifesto’s proposal on agentic commerce, interoperability and earlier fraud prevention as examples of how industry collaboration can help strengthen the UK’s payments sector by 2030. 
Emma Banymandhub, CEO of The Payments Association, said: “The assumption that payments can run on autopilot while facing mounting fraud and digital disruption has to end. Payments are the vital economic lifeblood keeping society functioning. If money stopped moving for even five minutes, the fallout would be significant. We aren't just presenting a wish list. Our members are stepping up to deliver the accountability, infrastructure and cross-sector collaboration required to future-proof the UK economy." 
Renuka Rawlins, Director of Policy and Government Relations at The Payments Association, commented: “The challenge now is turning policy ambition into practical progress. This Manifesto identifies where industry, government and regulators need to work together to deliver meaningful change. The Payments Association will help convene that collaboration, develop the evidence needed to inform decisions and track progress against the priorities as we work towards 2030.” 
The Manifesto’s eight policy recommendations cover the modernisation of UK payments infrastructure; international competitiveness for payments businesses; earlier fraud prevention through actionable intelligence sharing; financial inclusion and meaningful payment choice; trusted rules for agentic payments; internationally interoperable standards for agentic commerce; proportionate regulation for next-generation payments; and interoperability between existing and emerging forms of regulated money.

title: Klarna Goes Global With Anti-Scam Call Verification
summary:
Klarna, the everyday finance network, today announced its popular in-app Call Status Detection tool is now live globally, giving consumers a reliable and simple way to check whether someone calling them is genuinely from Klarna.
Call Status Detection has already helped thousands of consumers verify calls since it launched in the Nordics  in September. The feature has now been rolled out globally, reflecting Klarna’s commitment to protecting its customers from fraud.
Call Status Detection is quick and easy to use by design. If a customer takes a call from someone claiming to be Klarna, all they have to do is open the Klarna app and check the banner at the top of their screen — green means the call is verified and it is safe to continue, while amber means Klarna cannot verify the call and the customer should hang up.
The feature builds on Klarna’s existing anti-fraud measures like the Klarna Inbox, which enables verification of written communication like emails, texts and letters, and aims to protect customers by making it harder for scammers to impersonate Klarna. 
“Scammers are a global problem, so our protections need to be too,” said Klarna Head of Financial Crime Woody Malouf. “Every Klarna customer now gets the same simple check. No need to hunt for a number, just open the app, look at the colour, and you know whether it’s safe to keep talking.”
Fraudsters impersonating banks and payment providers over the phone has become one of the fastest-growing threats to consumers, and caller ID can be spoofed easily. Fraudsters stole an estimated $579 billion worldwide through scams and bank fraud in 2025, according to Nasdaq Verafin.
Call Status Detection will be enabled by default in the Klarna app for iOS users in all 26 markets where Klarna operates. Android users will need to enable the feature in their Klarna app settings.

title: LexisNexis Risk Solutions Extends Risk Intelligence to Agentic Activity
summary:
LexisNexis® Risk Solutions has extended its powerful risk intelligence solutions to help organisations understand and assess a new class of digital actor: AI agents operating on behalf of people and businesses.
For decades, LexisNexis Risk Solutions has helped organisations make risk decisions by connecting identity, device, behavioural, network and transaction intelligence at global scale. As AI agents become another participant in digital interactions, the company is extending that same connected intelligence approach to agentic activity.
Know Your Agent (KYA) intelligence adds a new layer of agentic insights to LexisNexis Risk Solutions’ digital identity and fraud prevention platform. It helps organisations recognise when AI agents are interacting with their digital services and can bring those interactions directly into established risk assessment and decisioning workflows, rather than treating them as an isolated risk problem. Many LexisNexis Risk Solutions customers are already using KYA intelligence in their current risk management decision making.
Analysis of global digital transactions by LexisNexis Risk Solutions shows agentic traffic grew over 750% in the first half of 2026 alone. Rapid growth is expected to continue as more people and organisations adopt agents to undertake everyday tasks such as online shopping.
Because most personal agents today do not self-declare as agents, organisations face an immediate challenge: distinguishing agentic activity from other digital traffic. But this is only the first step. Agent detection alone cannot answer key questions organisations ultimately need to resolve: Who or what is the agent acting for? Has that activity been authorised? Is its behaviour consistent with that authority? And does the wider context of the interaction indicate that it is legitimate?
That context may also change during a digital journey as control passes between a person and an AI agent, making continuous visibility into the interaction increasingly important. This is where the scale and connectivity of the Risk Intelligence Network becomes essential.
AI-agent activity does not need to be evaluated as an isolated interaction. It can be understood in the context of the identities, devices, networks, behavioural patterns and relationships surrounding digital activity, helping to provide richer context for risk decisions. This connected intelligence approach incorporates agent detection into risk decisions in real time, while aiding in creating a foundation for increasingly sophisticated agent identity and authorisation capabilities as agents, standards and use cases evolve.
Autonomous AI agents have the potential to increase the scale and sophistication of fraud, including authorised push payment fraud and account takeover attacks. Malicious agents can learn dynamically from successes and failures, enabling subsequent attacks to become more tailored and prolific.
For organisations, the decision is not whether an agent is universally trusted but whether a specific agent, acting in a specific context, should be permitted to perform a specific action. Legitimate agents will increasingly participate in digital customer journeys, but the appropriate response will depend on what the agent is attempting to do, the context of the interaction, and the organisation’s own risk policies. KYA intelligence helps organisations bring agentic activity into existing decisioning workflows so they can allow, authenticate, review or reject interactions as appropriate.
“Agentic commerce is moving quickly from experimentation into the mainstream,” said Grayson Clarke, chief commercial officer at LexisNexis Risk Solutions. “Agentic transactions globally more than doubled again in the last quarter, driven primarily by personal agents. Some businesses are enabling agents to transact on consumers’ behalf, while others are restricting their activities, and many are still determining the right approach. We have already seen firsthand how a global financial institution used our detection capabilities to help identify agentic activity and prevent it from executing sensitive transactions.”
LexisNexis Risk Solutions analysed more than 116 billion digital transactions globally in 2025 through its LexisNexis® Digital Identity Network®, giving it a uniquely broad view of how human, automated and increasingly agentic interactions are evolving. The network detected 4.9 billion automated bot attacks during the year, a 59% increase year over year. That scale reflects the role LexisNexis Risk Solutions already plays in helping many of the world's largest financial institutions, merchants and digital businesses assess risk across digital interactions.
Mike Woodberry, senior vice president of product and analytics at LexisNexis Risk Solutions, added, “Managing risk in the agentic economy will require more than agent detection alone. The real challenge is establishing context: what is acting, who or what it represents, whether it is authorised and what it is attempting to do. Our vision for KYA is to extend established risk intelligence into the agentic economy, helping give organisations the flexibility to apply the appropriate response to each interaction rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all risk assessment.”
Woodberry continued, “Organisations should not have to build a new risk strategy every time digital interactions evolve. Adding a new layer of agentic insights to our established identity and fraud prevention platform helps customers build on the capabilities they already rely on while preparing for the next generation of digital interactions.”

title: Nexi and Deutsche Telekom Selected by the European Central Bank to Provide Digital Euro Network Service Provider (NSP) Connectivity
summary:
Nexi, in temporary grouping with Deutsche Telekom, has been selected by the European Central Bank (ECB) as one of the two successful tenderers, for the provision of Network Service Provider (NSP) Connectivity for the digital euro, and the one providing NSP services to support the pilot project. This announcement follows the conclusion of the ECB's negotiated public procurement procedure to select contractors for the provision of secure, reliable, and high-performance connectivity services for the future digital currency.
The implementation of this high-performance network—which will interconnect the data centers hosting the components of the Digital Euro Service Platform (DESP) as well as enable crucial external actors such as Payment Service Providers (PSPs) and National Central Banks to access the Digital Euro Service Platform (DESP)—is a foundational pillar for the successful launch and operation of the digital euro project.
The joint solution proposed by Nexi and Deutsche Telekom offers a robust and scalable connectivity and mediation platform designed to enable the end-to-end exchange of digital euro transactions across the entire DESP ecosystem. Engineered to guarantee the smooth delivery of digital euro services to end-users, the architecture supports high levels of scalability and elasticity, allowing resources to be adjusted efficiently to meet varying transaction volumes and peak usage scenarios.
The total duration of the service agreement is ten years from the contract's official start date.
